titleZh: 酒店早餐浪费多，先减品种还是先改补餐方式？
titleEn: Hotel Breakfast Waste: Reduce the Menu or Adjust Replenishment?
summaryZh: 早餐剩余偏多时，先分辨备餐、餐台还是客盘环节，再判断应调品种、出品量或补餐节奏，并同时检查成本、供餐和人工。
summaryEn: When breakfast waste appears high, a hotel should first identify whether it occurs in preparation, on the buffet or on guests’ plates. Then it can decide whether to adjust the menu, batch sizes or replenishment timing while checking food cost, service availability and labor.
contentZh:
酒店早餐浪费多，先减品种还是先改补餐方式？

早餐收餐时，餐台上还剩着不少食物，总经理很容易想到：是不是品种太多，明天少做几样？但如果同一场早餐里，晚到的客人又反映想吃的东西已经没有了，就不能只凭收餐时的剩余量决定删菜单。

这两个现象可能同时发生：不受欢迎的品项做多了，客人需要的品项却补晚了。早餐减浪费，应该先分清剩余发生在备餐、餐台还是客盘，再判断该改品种、改出品数量，还是改补餐节奏。品种可以减，但要知道减掉的究竟是低需求供给，还是客人仍然需要的选择。

先弄清食物为什么剩下

雅高在2026年10月9日发布的可持续餐饮介绍中，提到通过记录被丢弃食材及浪费发生的时间，帮助厨房调整日常操作。希尔顿2025年4月30日介绍的Green Breakfast项目，也把早餐减废与过量生产识别、服务方式调整联系起来。

这些公开实践支持酒店先测量、再调整的思路，但不能证明每家酒店都该减少相同品种，更不能把境外项目的减废效果直接写进本店预算。真正决定动作的，仍是本店食物在哪里剩下，以及当时的客人有没有得到应有的服务。

建议把需要调查的剩余分开记录。

备餐剩余，是已经为早餐准备、最终没有进入餐台的部分。这里要核对预计就餐人数、实际到店人数，以及一次准备的数量。含早房间数不能直接当作就餐人数；住客是否用餐、儿童和外来用餐者如何计入，都需要统一口径。

餐台剩余，是已经摆出、收餐时仍未被取用的部分。它可能与品项需求不足有关，也可能出在最后一轮补得太多，或者没有根据后续客流调整出品。只有知道什么时候补了多少，才能区分这两种情况。

客盘剩余，是客人取走后没有吃完的部分。它需要结合份量、口味、温度、取餐便利和现场反馈分析。仅凭盘里剩了某种食物，不能认定客人不喜欢，更不能立即取消这个品项。

这几类记录用于诊断，不改变酒店已有的食品安全要求。食物是否可以继续保存或使用，须按适用规定和本店食品安全程序处理；减废不能成为放宽要求的理由。

什么时候调品种，什么时候调补餐

如果某个品项在客流相近的多场早餐中，始终取用很少、餐台剩余较多，才值得进一步检查它是否与其他品项重复、是否不适合主要客群，以及展示或出品质量有没有问题。排除这些因素后，可以评估减少初始出品量、轮换供应，或者调整品种。

但取用少，不一定意味着可以删除。为特定饮食需求提供的选择，或品牌与已售套餐承诺的内容，即使数量小，也可能需要保留。总经理应先明确哪些供应是必须兑现的，不能让厨房只按销量自行取舍。

如果一个品项前半场取用正常，剩余主要出现在最后一轮补餐，更适合先调整补餐数量与时点。临近结束仍可能需要补餐，但可以根据尚未用餐的人数、现场取用速度和制作所需时间，决定补多少，而不是一律补满原来的大容器。

如果客盘剩余集中，单纯减少餐台供应未必有效。应先检查默认份量、口味反馈或出品状态。对可调整份量的品项，可以测试更小的单份供应，同时保留方便续取的方式，观察客人是否因此需要更多等待。

例如，一款热食品项在早餐高峰取用很快，临近收餐却经常剩下整盘。这里提出的是一个假设场景。它首先提示团队检查末段补餐，而不是认定这款食物不受欢迎。反过来，如果整个供应时段取用都很少，末段少补只能减少部分剩余，还需要回头检查品项本身。

把记录表放到一个具体品项上

开始时不必逐道菜全面称量。可以先选一组剩余明显、能够单独记录、又不会因试验影响必要供应的品项，由总厨和餐厅负责人共同跟踪。

一张早餐损耗与补餐记录表，至少应留下这些信息：日期与客群特点、分时实际就餐人数、品项名称、初始出品量、每次补餐时间与数量、备餐剩余、餐台剩余、客盘剩余，以及缺餐、等待和额外补餐工时。

剩余量与最终废弃量要分开记，同一批食物不能在多个环节重复累计。称量应扣除容器重量，区分可食部分与骨壳等不可食部分。若暂时只能记录整份数量，也应保持同一品项规格一致，不把不同口径混在一起比较。

可以把一行记录理解为：某日、某品项、某次补餐发生在什么时间，当时还有多少就餐需求，最后剩了多少，期间有没有客人等餐。首次记录时不知道的内容就留作待查，不用估数补齐。

客盘回收若难以准确分到单个品项，可先按能可靠识别的类别记录。数据粗一些但来源清楚，比看似精确、实际靠猜的数字更有用。

记录后，选择客群、星期和就餐规模较接近的场次作比较。先观察原来的做法，再只改一个因素，例如某品项末段的补餐批量。不要同时换菜单、缩短早餐时间、减少人手，否则很难解释变化来自哪里。遇到团队集中到店或临时增加的大批用餐需求，应单独标记，不能硬放进普通散客场次的比较中。

浪费少了，还要看客人和员工付出了什么

总废弃量下降，可能只是当天吃早餐的人少了。因此，应同时查看总量和每位实际就餐客人的废弃量，并保留客群与菜单变化记录。称重能帮助定位问题，不能直接代替财务核算；不同食物每公斤的成本并不相同。

财务可以按本店配方和采购成本估算相关食材价值，再核对后续出品与领料是否真正减少。废弃量下降未必立即变成采购支出下降，也不能只用食材节省额代表全部收益。

小批量补餐可能增加厨房制作次数、服务员往返和清洁工作。评估时，要把新增工时、能耗及耗材一并考虑。若省下的食材价值有限，却让早餐高峰更拥挤、员工频繁离开服务岗位，就需要重新调整做法。完成一轮可比场次后，由餐饮负责人和财务共同复核，再决定保留、调整还是恢复原方案；短期观察只支持这次操作选择，不能证明长期效果。

服务检查也应具体：在承诺的早餐时段内，必要品项是否可得；缺餐发生在哪些时段；客人等待有没有变长；晚到客人的选择是否明显不足。投诉可以提供线索，但没有投诉不等于没有问题，还要结合现场观察。

总经理负责划定服务承诺和调整权限，总厨负责出品与补餐方案，餐厅负责人记录客流和缺餐情况，财务核对食材与新增投入。开始试验前，应约定何种服务变化需要立即恢复原方案。涉及食品安全，或已经无法兑现既有供餐承诺时，应停止相关调整；不要等月底成本表出来后才处理。

小批量也不是所有酒店的答案

小型、有限服务酒店，如果厨房和餐厅由少量员工兼岗，频繁补餐可能挤占接待与清洁时间。此时更需要评估初始出品量、容器配置和可操作的补餐次数，不能照搬人员充足酒店的做法。

团队集中用餐、会议早餐或短时间内客流高度集中的场景，则需要保留足够的高峰供应。不能因为散客日的小批量试验有效，就直接压低团队早餐备餐量。

具备现场制作条件的酒店，可以评估部分品项按需制作，但前提是人员、设备和等待时间能够承受。没有这些条件时，按需制作也可能把食物损耗变成排队与投诉。

早餐减浪费，最后要回答的是：食物是否用得更合理，客人是否仍能在约定时间获得应有的早餐，团队是否有能力持续执行。下一次早餐，先选一组品项，把剩余发生的环节与补餐时点记清楚，再决定菜单上的哪一项需要改变。

资料来源：雅高，Creating Shared Value Through Sustainable Food，2026年10月9日；希尔顿，Serving Up Solutions: Hilton’s Efforts in Reducing Food Waste and Reimagining a More Responsible Plate，2025年4月30日。
contentEn:
Hotel Breakfast Waste: Reduce the Menu or Adjust Replenishment?

At the end of breakfast, food is still left on the buffet. A general manager may quickly conclude that there are too many items and decide to cut a few the next day. But if late-arriving guests at the same breakfast also report that the items they wanted were no longer available, the remaining food alone is not enough to justify cutting the menu.

Both conditions can occur at once: too much of a low-demand item was prepared, while a needed item was replenished too late. To reduce breakfast waste, first locate where it occurs: in preparation, on the buffet or on guests’ plates. Then decide whether to change the menu, the quantity prepared or the replenishment rhythm. Items can be removed, but the team should know whether it is removing low-demand supply or a choice guests still need.

First, find out why food is left over

In an update on sustainable food published on 9 October 2026, Accor described recording discarded ingredients and when waste occurs to help kitchens adjust daily practices. Hilton’s Green Breakfast initiative, described on 30 April 2025, also links breakfast waste reduction with identifying overproduction and adjusting service practices.

These public examples support measuring before making changes. They do not show that every hotel should reduce the same items, nor do results from overseas programs belong in an individual property’s budget. The decision depends on where food is left at this hotel and whether guests received the service they were promised.

Record the different types of leftovers separately.

Preparation surplus is food prepared for breakfast that never reaches the buffet. Check the expected and actual number of diners and the quantity prepared at one time. Rooms with breakfast included are not the same as actual diners. The property needs a consistent way to count guests who do not eat, children and outside diners.

Buffet surplus is food that was displayed but remains when service ends. It may indicate low demand for an item, an oversized final replenishment, or a failure to adjust output as traffic changed. Record when and how much was replenished to distinguish these causes.

Plate waste is food guests take but do not eat. Consider portion size, taste, temperature, ease of service and guest feedback. A partially eaten item alone does not prove that guests dislike it and is not a sufficient reason to remove it.

These records are diagnostic and do not change the hotel’s food-safety requirements. Whether food may be stored or used again must be handled under applicable rules and the property’s food-safety procedures. Waste reduction is never a reason to relax them.

When should the menu change, and when should replenishment change?

If an item is consistently taken in small quantities and leaves substantial buffet surplus across several breakfasts with comparable guest volumes, examine whether it duplicates another item, suits the main guest segments and is presented and prepared well. After checking these factors, consider reducing the initial batch, rotating the item or changing the menu.

Low take-up does not automatically mean an item should be removed. A choice that serves a specific dietary need, or is part of a brand or package promise, may need to remain even when demand is small. The general manager should identify what the hotel must provide; the kitchen should not make that decision on sales volume alone.

If an item is taken regularly earlier in service but surplus appears mainly after the final replenishment, first adjust its quantity and timing. Replenishment may still be necessary near closing. The team can decide how much to prepare based on the number of diners yet to arrive, the rate of take-up and the time needed to produce the item, rather than refilling a large container automatically.

If plate waste is concentrated on an item, simply reducing buffet supply may not help. Check the default portion, guest feedback and preparation quality. Where practical, test a smaller serving while keeping a convenient way to take more, and observe whether guests have to wait longer.

For example, a hot item may be taken quickly during the breakfast peak but remain in a full tray near closing. This is a hypothetical scenario. It points first to checking the final replenishment, not to assuming the item is unpopular. Conversely, if take-up is low throughout service, reducing the final batch addresses only part of the surplus; the item itself also needs review.

Use a record sheet for a specific item

There is no need to weigh every dish at the outset. Select a small group of clearly identifiable items with visible surplus that can be tracked without jeopardizing necessary service. The executive chef and restaurant lead can follow them together.

A breakfast waste and replenishment record should include at least: date and guest mix; actual diners by time period; item; initial quantity; time and quantity of each replenishment; preparation surplus; buffet surplus; plate waste; shortages, waiting and additional replenishment labor.

Record leftover quantities separately from food ultimately discarded. Do not count the same batch more than once at different stages. Deduct container weight and distinguish edible food from bones and shells. If the team can only count portions at first, keep portion sizes consistent and do not compare unlike measures.

One record can capture the date, item, replenishment time, demand remaining at that moment, final surplus and any guest waiting. If something is unknown during the first pass, mark it for follow-up instead of estimating it.

If plate returns cannot be reliably assigned to individual items, begin with the categories the team can identify. Rough data with a clear source are more useful than precise-looking guesses.

After recording, compare breakfasts with similar guest mix, day of week and diner volume. Observe the current practice first, then change one factor only, such as the final replenishment batch. Do not change the menu, shorten breakfast hours and reduce staffing at the same time; the team would not know what caused the result. Mark large group arrivals or sudden volume changes separately rather than comparing them with ordinary leisure or individual guest mornings.

Less waste should not come at the expense of guests or staff

A fall in total discarded food may simply reflect fewer diners. Review both total waste and waste per actual diner, and keep a note of changes in guest mix and menu. Weighing helps locate a problem, but it does not replace financial analysis; a kilogram of one food does not cost the same as a kilogram of another.

Finance can estimate the value of ingredients using the property’s recipes and purchase costs, then check whether subsequent production and requisitions actually declined. Less discarded food does not necessarily reduce purchasing costs immediately, and ingredient savings alone do not represent the full result.

Smaller replenishment batches may increase kitchen production cycles, staff trips and cleaning. Include additional labor, energy and consumables in the review. If the ingredient value saved is small but the breakfast peak becomes more congested and employees leave service positions more often, revise the approach. After a comparable set of service periods, the food-and-beverage lead and finance should review the result together and decide whether to keep, adjust or reverse the change. Short-term observation supports an operating decision; it does not establish a long-term effect.

Make the service checks specific: Were necessary items available during the promised breakfast hours? When did shortages occur? Did waiting increase? Did late-arriving guests have materially fewer choices? Complaints can provide clues, but the absence of complaints does not prove that service was adequate; observe the operation as well.

The general manager sets service commitments and approval limits. The executive chef owns the production and replenishment plan. The restaurant lead records traffic and shortages. Finance checks ingredient costs and additional inputs. Before a test begins, agree what service change would trigger an immediate return to the original plan. Stop an adjustment if it creates a food-safety concern or prevents the hotel from meeting an existing service commitment. Do not wait for the month-end cost report.

Smaller batches are not right for every hotel

In a small, limited-service hotel where a few employees cover both kitchen and restaurant duties, frequent replenishment may pull staff away from reception or cleaning. Review the initial batch, serving containers and the number of feasible replenishments. Do not copy the practice of a larger hotel with more staff.

Hotels serving concentrated group breakfasts, meetings or a short, sharp demand peak need enough supply for that peak. A small-batch test that works on an individual-traveler morning does not justify cutting preparation for a group breakfast.

A hotel with suitable equipment and staffing can consider preparing some items to order, provided waiting time and workload remain manageable. Without those conditions, made-to-order service may turn food waste into queues and complaints.

The final test is whether food is used more appropriately, guests still receive the breakfast promised during the stated service hours, and the team can keep the process running. At the next breakfast, choose a small group of items, record where surplus occurs and when replenishment takes place, then decide which menu or operating change is justified.

Sources: Accor, “Creating Shared Value Through Sustainable Food,” 9 October 2026; Hilton, “Serving Up Solutions: Hilton’s Efforts in Reducing Food Waste and Reimagining a More Responsible Plate,” 30 April 2025.

FAQ

Q: Should a hotel remove menu items to reduce breakfast waste?
A: Not before identifying whether surplus comes from preparation, the buffet or guests’ plates. Compare similar service periods, check guest commitments and demand, then change one factor at a time.

Q: What should a breakfast waste record include?
A: Actual diners by time period, initial production, replenishment times and quantities, preparation surplus, buffet surplus, plate waste, shortages, waiting and additional labor. Keep the measures consistent and avoid counting the same food twice.

Q: How can the hotel tell whether a change worked?
A: Compare similar breakfasts and review waste per actual diner, ingredient value, shortages, waiting and additional labor together. A lower waste total alone does not prove improved profit or service.

Q: Should every hotel use smaller replenishment batches?
A: No. Limited staffing, concentrated group arrivals, equipment and service commitments affect what is practical. Test the method in a suitable period and restore the previous approach if service or safety is affected.
author: 迈创兄弟C&T
